newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman holds talks with Serb leaders in enclave.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman holds talks with Serb leaders in enclave.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman visited Croatia's last Serb enclave on Monday to underscore in talks with local Serb officials that the peaceful return of Eastern Slavonia to Zagreb rule was going well.

After the meeting, he was prevented by security men from speaking to the public as he had planned. Around 100 young men were gathered in the town square and shouted insults as Tudjman got into his car and sped away.
He made no statement about the contents of his discussion.

The visit followed municipal elections in April, in which Serbs from the region took part in a Croatian vote for the first time since 1991, when they went to war over Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia and seized around a third of the country.

Beli Manastir had a Croatian majority before the war but now lies in the only Serb majority region in the country -- now administered by the United Nations. The current U.N. mandate ends on July 15 and Eastern Slavonia is then due to come under Croatian government control.
Zagreb recaptured all other Serb areas in a lightning offensive in 1995.

However the United States has led Western criticism of Croatia's progress with commitments made under the Bosnian peace treaty signed in 1995 and has hinted it might call for the current mandate covering 5,000 troops to be extended.
The U.N. Security Council will vote soon on whether the present mandate will be prolonged or whether it will be reduced to a purely monitoring mission with fewer troops.
Croatia has already agreed that some form of U.N. presence can remain until January next year.
Beli Manastir is the second largest town in the region after Vukovar, which was flattened during fighting in 1991.
Tudjman met leaders of the Independent Serbian Democratic Party (SDSS) and the newly-elected Serb mayor of Beli Manastir.
A U.N. spokesman told Reuters peacekeepers had stepped up security measures and said the whole area was under control.
Tudjman, who is expected to win a June 15 presidential election, paid a surprise first visit to Vukovar last December after his return from medical treatment in the United States.
